summary: The abstract, introduction and conclusion match the body on the headline counts. Those are 70 hits, 34 unique articles, 3,187 coded articles, 92 relevant articles, 43 projects, 29 projects dated to the day or month, 14 of 15 counties, 700 579 listings and 38 percent of listings mentioning cycling. They also omit or overstate several body caveats. The abstract says the data can be linked to housing listings, but Section 6.1 says the listings have not been linked. The 97 percent agreement figure is given without the body's warning that the validation sample is too small for any comparison. The full-run counts and the conclusion's "demonstrated" language leave out that the full run is unvalidated and that several steps were done by hand. The introduction's "scalable pipeline for creating treatment data" conflicts with the manual steps and the non-random date precision reported later. The abstract's "only two actual openings" is stale against a Table 2 footnote showing a third opening occurred. The abstract's generalisation from one search term also lacks a caveat. Section 6 uses 44 projects and 96 articles, including a project both coders marked not relevant.

findings.finding_summary: The abstract says the paper shows how the data can be linked to 700 579 FINN.no listings, but Section 6.1 states that no linkage was done and the listings are only described in Appendix A.

location.text_quote: Finally, we show how the data can be linked to 700 579 housing listings from FINN.no

findings.claim_text: The abstract claims that the paper shows how the newspaper-based data can be linked to 700 579 housing listings from FINN.no.
findings.evidence_summary: Section 6.1 and Appendix A describe the listings, compute the share mentioning cycling (38 percent) and propose models in Section 6.3. Section 6.1 says explicitly 'We have not yet linked the listings to the database.' Section 8 lists linkage as a future step. Only the descriptive listing statistics and the proposed models are in the paper. No linkage or demonstration of linkage is. The abstract's 'propose models' clause is accurate, but 'show how the data can be linked' reads as a delivered result.

findings.finding_summary: The abstract reports 97 percent human–LLM agreement as 'the same rate as between two human coders' without the body's warning that the 34-article, 3-relevant sample is too small to compare the rates and is indicative only.

findings.claim_text: On the pilot, the LLM agrees with a human coder on the relevance of 97 percent of the articles, the same rate as between two human coders, and gives the same opening date for all three relevant articles.
findings.evidence_summary: The figures match Tables 3 and 4 (33 of 34 articles in each). Section 4 states that with only 34 articles, of which 3 were coded relevant, 'the sample is too small to test whether the two agreement rates differ' and that 'The results are thus indicative only.' The agreement is driven by 30 articles both coded not relevant. In each table only 3 relevant articles carry the relevance signal, and the date comparison also rests on those 3. The abstract and the introduction (which says 'very close to the rate between the two human coders') contain none of this caveat. Section 8 repeats it.

The Section 8 caveats do appear in the paper, so this is an omission from the conclusion, not a contradiction.

findings.evidence_summary: The counts match Section 5 and Table 6 (19 + 10 = 29 projects dated to day or month; 19 + 10 + 9 + 5 = 43 projects). Section 8 says 'a random sample from the full run of 3,187 articles should also be checked against human coding', so precision and recall in the full run are unmeasured. The pilot validation set is the only accuracy evidence. In it, 1 of the 4 LLM-relevant articles (the Stord article) was not relevant per the pilot coder (Table 4). Section 8 also says grouping articles into projects was done by hand. The abstract and conclusion give the counts without noting that no accuracy estimate exists for the full run. I cannot determine the full-run error rate from the manuscript.

findings.finding_summary: The abstract generalises from a 70-hit pilot using a single search term to the conclusion that 'keyword search alone is too noisy and that an LLM filter is needed', although the body presents this as the pilot's low yield and tests no non-LLM filter.

findings.claim_text: A pilot of 70 search hits contained only two actual openings, showing that keyword search alone is too noisy and that an LLM filter is needed.
findings.evidence_summary: Section 3.1.2 describes a 70-hit sample from 2 September to 10 October 2026. Section 3.1.1 says the search term was 'sykkelvei'. The body words the conclusion more cautiously: 'The low yield points to the need for an LLM to filter the articles'. The body also says other keyword choices give between about 530 and 13 800 hits in three years. The pilot does not compare other search terms or non-LLM filters such as date or phrase rules. It also shows the LLM filter flagged one non-relevant article (Table 4). The abstract's 'showing' and 'is needed' are stronger than 'points to' for one term and one five-week sample.

findings.finding_summary: The introduction describes the contribution as 'a scalable pipeline for creating treatment data', but Sections 6.3 and 8 report non-random date precision and manual grouping and linking steps that qualify that description.

findings.claim_text: Our contribution is a scalable pipeline for creating treatment data for research questions that are currently difficult to study.
findings.evidence_summary: Section 5 and Table 6 show 29 of 43 projects dated to day or month and 14 only to year or not stated. Section 6.3 reports that 17 of 18 projects with a reported ceremony are dated to the day, against 2 of 26 without, and says 'This suggests that the precision of the dates is not random'. Section 6.3 adds that this could bias results toward zero in the proposed housing design. Section 8 says grouping articles into projects and matching projects to NVDB segments were done by hand and 'should be automated', and that several steps 'remain before the database can be used for causal research'. The introduction's 'scalable' and 'treatment data' wording and the abstract's emphasis on causal research do not carry these qualifications. The API cost of NOK 70 is reported, but the hand steps limit what has been shown to scale.

findings.evidence_summary: The abstract, Section 5, Table 6 and the conclusion give 92 articles and 43 projects. Section 6 gives 96 articles and 44 projects, and Table 7 uses 44 projects. Footnote 3 explains the difference as four pilot articles and the Stord project. It also says the Stord project 'was coded as not relevant by both human coders'. Section 6 says all 96 records 'reported an opening', which conflicts with the footnote and with Section 4, where the Stord article mentions a path completed the year before only in passing. The pilot articles' overlap with rounds 2–4 is not described. The two sets of counts are labelled, but a reader cannot tell which figure applies without the footnote, and the 44 includes a project that did not report an opening.

notes: Parser-quality guidance was followed. Structured table CSV/markdown objects were not used as evidence. All quotes come from the page text files, which parser-quality review found safe.

Abstract and body headline counts were checked and agree: 70 hits, 34 unique articles, 3,187 coded articles, 92 relevant articles, 43 projects, 19+10=29 projects dated to day or month, 14 of 15 counties, 700 579 listings, 38 percent. The agreement figure of 33 of 34 articles is also consistent across Tables 3 and 4 and the text.

The abstract's NVDB sentence is scoped to 'one opening' and matches Section 4.3, so no finding was raised on it. Section 8 notes that systematic comparison is still needed to measure how much the articles add.
